Whether or not the trout habitat in the main body of Jocassee Reservoir would be eliminated under the combined operation of the Jocassee and Bad Creek Projects would depend on the operating plant factors of the projects and the amounts of cooler water they remove from the reservoir. Under the proposed plan of operation for both projects, however, it is expected that the optimum habitat (20°C; 5 mg/1 DO) would be eliminated in the main body of the reservoir.
The reductions in trout habitat discussed above refer to the optimum coldwater habitat as defined by 20°C and 5.0 mg/l of DO. As discussed earlier (Section 2.2.2.2), trout would be expected to survive under more restricted habitat criterion, in particular, lower DO level. Using minimum habitat criterion of 21°C and 3.0 mg/l DO, the effect of Jocassee and Bad Creek operation would be to cause a reduction in this habitat also. However, insufficient data are available to determine the extent of this reduction and whether or not such habitat would be totally eliminated.
The average tributary flow into Jocassee Reservoir is about 460 cfs, 350 cfs, 400 cfs, and 350 cfs for June, July, August, and September, respectively. Although it is expected that the coldwater habitat in the main body of Jocassee would be lost under full operation of the Jocassee and Pad Creek Projects, the inflow might maintain a small amount of trout habitat in the arms of the main tributaries of the reservoir.
Operation of the proposed Bad Creek facility would result in entrainment of some Lake Jocassee fishes. During pumpback operations, velocity at the inlet would reach a maximum average of 5.6 feet per second. During generation, maximum velocity at the inlet would be 9.2 feet per second in the upper reservoir.
Studies evaluating mortality of fish passing through pump turbines (Serchuk, 1976) have shown pumping mode average mortalities of 56.5 to 65.1 percent. Of these, 37.2 to 61.5 percent showed physical damage. Generation tests showed 35.4 to 74.8 percent mortality with 47.8 percent of the fish showing damage. Large fish would suffer greater mortality than smaller ones.
